## ARGUMENT

**Officer [Name] Is Entitled to Qualified Immunity Because No Clearly Established Law Prohibited Using a Taser on an Actively Resisting Suspect.**

Qualified immunity shields an officer unless existing precedent placed the unlawfulness of his conduct "beyond debate." *Ashcroft v. al-Kidd*, 563 U.S. 731, 741 (2011). Plaintiff bears the burden of showing that the asserted right was clearly established. *See Arrington-Bey v. City of Bedford Heights*, 858 F.3d 988, 992 (6th Cir. 2017). General statements that officers may not use excessive force will not do. Plaintiff must identify precedent with a sufficiently similar fact pattern to give a reasonable officer fair and clear warning that this use of force was unlawful. *Id.* at 992–93. Plaintiff cannot.

**A. Circuit precedent permits using a taser to subdue an actively resisting suspect.**

The reasonableness of force is judged from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene, with attention to the severity of the crime, the threat to officers or others, and whether the suspect is actively resisting arrest or attempting to flee. *Graham v. Connor*, 490 U.S. 386, 396 (1989). In taser cases, active resistance is the critical dividing line.

In *Hagans v. Franklin County Sheriff's Office*, 695 F.3d 505 (6th Cir. 2012), a deputy used a taser on a suspect who was resisting officers' efforts to handcuff him. The Sixth Circuit held that the deputy was entitled to qualified immunity because no clearly established law forbade that use of force. *Id.* at 508–11. Surveying the case law, the court explained that when a suspect actively resists arrest and refuses to be handcuffed, officers do not violate the Fourth Amendment by using a taser to subdue him. *Id.* at 509–10.

*Rudlaff v. Gillispie*, 791 F.3d 638 (6th Cir. 2015), confirms the rule. Officers used a knee strike and a taser on a man who physically resisted arrest, and the court held that they were entitled to qualified immunity. *Id.* at 641–44. It drew a straightforward line: police may use a taser to subdue a suspect who is actively resisting arrest, but not one who is not resisting or has stopped resisting. *Id.* at 642.

The same result follows here. [Insert record facts showing active resistance at the time of each taser application, such as pulling away, struggling against handcuffing, or fleeing, with record citations.] Far from clearly prohibiting Officer [Name]'s response to that conduct, *Hagans* and *Rudlaff* support it. At a minimum, a reasonable officer could conclude that deploying a taser in these circumstances was lawful.

**B. Decisions involving suspects who were not actively resisting cannot clearly establish a right here.**

Cases denying immunity for taser use are materially different when they turn on the absence of active resistance. In *Kent v. Oakland County*, 810 F.3d 384 (6th Cir. 2016), the plaintiff was tased while against a wall with his hands raised. Although he had not complied with officers' commands, he was not actively resisting, and the court denied immunity. *See id.* at 392, 396–97. Similarly, *Goodwin v. City of Painesville*, 781 F.3d 314 (6th Cir. 2015), denied immunity where, viewing the evidence in the plaintiff's favor, the person tased was not actively resisting. *See id.* at 323–27. And *Austin v. Redford Township Police Department*, 690 F.3d 490 (6th Cir. 2012), addressed taser use on a suspect who, on the facts viewed in his favor, had already been apprehended and was no longer resisting. *See id.* at 496–99.

None of these decisions would tell a reasonable officer that he may not tase a suspect who is still actively resisting. To the contrary, they are consistent with the line reflected in *Hagans* and *Rudlaff*. Because Plaintiff cannot show that clearly established law prohibited Officer [Name]'s conduct, Officer [Name] is entitled to qualified immunity.
